Page title: How a Lighthouse Lens Works
<<<PAGE TEXT START>>>
A lighthouse lamp on its own is weak. A single bright flame, even a strong one, spreads its glow in every direction and fades before it reaches a ship over the horizon. The trick that made lighthouses useful for ships far out at sea was not a stronger flame but a better way of aiming the light that already existed.

In 1822 the French engineer Augustin Fresnel built a lens that did exactly this. Instead of one thick piece of curved glass, which would have been very heavy, he used many thin glass rings and prisms arranged in a circle. Each ring bends the light from the lamp at the centre so that it leaves in a flat, narrow beam instead of spreading out. The result is a lens that is far lighter than a solid one and captures much more of the lamp's light.

Large lenses of this kind turn slowly on a bed of liquid mercury or on ball bearings, driven by a clockwork motor. As the lens turns, its beams sweep across the sea like the spokes of a wheel. A sailor watching from a ship sees a brief flash each time a beam passes, which is why most lighthouses flash rather than shine steadily.

The time between flashes is a signature. One tower may flash once every ten seconds and its neighbour twice every fifteen, so a navigator can identify the light on a chart. Some lights use red or green panels to mark dangerous sectors, so that a ship sees a white light while on a safe course and a coloured one when it drifts toward rocks.

Modern lights often use small electric lamps and plastic lenses, and many have no keeper. But the oldest Fresnel lenses, some of which are still working after more than a century, remain a good example of solving an engineering problem with geometry instead of brute force.

Page title: Lighthouses: A Short History of Light on the Coast
<<<PAGE TEXT START>>>
Building a lighthouse on land is hard enough, but the most dangerous rocks lie well offshore, where the sea breaks over them in every storm. The Eddystone Rocks, about fourteen miles off the coast of Plymouth in England, were a notorious trap for ships entering the English Channel. The first tower there was a wooden structure begun in 1696 by Henry Winstanley, and it was swept away in a great storm in 1703 with Winstanley inside it. A second tower, built by John Rudyerd, lasted until it burned down in 1755. The third, built by John Smeaton and finished in 1759, changed the field. Smeaton studied the shape of an oak tree, which is wide at the base and narrows as it rises, and cut his granite blocks to lock together like dovetailed joints. His tower stood for more than a century, and its design was copied around the world.

Argand lamps and reflectors

Better towers needed better lamps. In the 1780s the Swiss scientist Aime Argand invented an oil lamp with a hollow circular wick, which let air reach the flame from both inside and out. The result burned far brighter and cleaner than an ordinary wick, and lighthouse builders soon adopted it. They placed these lamps in front of curved metal mirrors, usually made of silvered copper, to throw the light in one direction instead of letting it spread. Scotland's Stevenson family of engineers, who built many of the country's lighthouses, including the Bell Rock light in 1810, used such lamps and mirrors extensively. The system worked, but it needed constant polishing, because soot dulled the mirrors, and a lot of light was still lost around the edges. The next step came from a French physicist who looked at the problem in an entirely new way.

Fresnel's lens

In the 1820s the French engineer Augustin Fresnel designed a lens made of many glass rings and prisms arranged around a central lamp. A solid glass lens large enough to gather the light of a lighthouse lamp would have been too heavy to build or turn. Fresnel's stepped design kept only the parts of the glass that actually bend the light, and it made the lens thin and light. It captured much more of the lamp's output and sent it out as a narrow, powerful beam. The first Fresnel lens was installed at the Cordouan lighthouse in France in 1823, and within a few decades the design had spread to nearly every major light. Lenses came in sizes called orders, from the huge first order, taller than a person, down to small sixth order lenses for harbours. Many are still in use today, and a few still turn on their original mechanisms.
